title: Oscar-Nominated Animator Theodore Ushev to Present Adaptation of Shane Jones’ Cult Novel ‘Light Boxes’ in Venice
description: Bulgarian filmmaker Theodore Ushev, Oscar-nominated in the animated short film category in 2017 for “Blind Vaysha,” is in pre-production on feature
body:
Bulgarian filmmaker Theodore Ushev, Oscar-nominated in the animated short film category in 2017 for “Blind Vaysha,” is in pre-production on feature film “Light Boxes,” which he will present at the Venice Production Bridge’s Gap-Financing Market, running Sept. 4-6.

	The film, which will include stop-motion animation and live-action sequences, is an adaptation of Shane Jones’ cult novel exploring the tension between escaping war through imagination and confronting its reality.
	

	Set in a war-torn Ukrainian town, the story follows Anna, a 13-year-old girl who, despite restrictions imposed by Russian occupying forces, ventures into a ruined library and rescues a burning book titled “Light Boxes.”


	Seeking refuge from constant bombardment, Anna discovers Bianca, her imaginary double, living in a fantastical town imprisoned by a war of its own. There, the tyrannical February has condemned its inhabitants to eternal winter and forbids them from flying, while a masked resistance movement known as The Solution fights to restore light and freedom.

	With neither reality nor imagination offering an escape from tyranny, the film asks whether hope, memory and love can persevere when war threatens to extinguish them all.

	For Ushev, survival lies in imitation. “The characters are constantly trying to reproduce what they have lost to convince themselves it can somehow return,” he tells Variety. “That is what I find fascinating about every totalitarian regime – no matter how oppressed people become, they will always find ways to recreate what has been taken from them, to keep hope alive.”
	

	Until “Light Boxes,” the director had never wanted to make an animated feature, believing a project of such scale would “risk the individual touch, the imperfection” that defined his work. That changed in 2010, when, while presenting his short “Lipsett Diaries” in Toronto, he stumbled upon Jones’ novel. “As soon as I read ‘Light Boxes,’ I immediately imagined how I would recreate it with puppets,” he recalls.

	Producer Jacqueline Wagenstein, founder of lead production company Cinelibri, acquired the adaptation rights, previously held by American filmmaker Spike Jonze, and set the fable up as a five-country co-production between Bulgaria, Canada, France, Belgium and Poland. The project is to become the largest Bulgarian-led animated feature production to date.

	Visually, “Light Boxes” will distinguish its two worlds through different media: Anna’s reality will unfold in live action with a predominantly Ukrainian cast, while Bianca’s world will be rendered in stop-motion using puppets designed and crafted by Ushev. “Bianca’s world will be the main one,” he explains. “For me, the puppet animation is at the heart of the film.”

	Symbols are at the story’s core. With natural light extinguished, its inhabitants recreate it through floating lights, drifting dandelions and artificial suns – man-made substitutes for the warmth and hope their world no longer provides. “Lighting will play a very important role in how we shoot the film, but also in the sets themselves. The materials used to build them will include fabrics recycled from parachutes, kites and other objects designed to fly,” comments the director.

	That symbolism extends to February’s ban on flight, which Ushev sees as stripping people of their capacity to dream. “When you fly, you dream,” he says. “And the first thing every tyrant does is take away people’s dreams – their hope that things can change.”

	The film acts as a reminder that preserving the light requires more than hoping it will endure. “The present is crucial to what happens in our future,” he says. “If we don’t act now and change things, then the future will also exist in the dark.”

title: Camilo Séptimo Keyboardist Jonathan Meléndez, His Pregnant Wife and 3-Year Old Daughter Murdered in Mexico
description: Jonathan Meléndez, keyboardist for the Mexican group Camilo Séptimo, his wife, 3-year-old daughter, and nanny were found murdered at their home near
body:
Jonathan Meléndez, keyboardist for the Mexican group Camilo Séptimo, his wife, 3-year-old daughter, and nanny were found murdered at their home near Mexico City, according to a statement from the State of Mexico Prosecutor’s Office and CNN.

	Ana Paula Meléndez, 35, was four months pregnant, according to authorities; a 6-year-old child was also found alive and unharmed inside the home, which is located in a residential complex in the municipality of Atizapán de Zaragoza residential complex.
	

	“The victims, a 38-year-old male, music producer and songwriter identified by the initials J.S.M.O., his 35-year-old pregnant wife, their 3-year-old daughter, and a 21-year-old female,” the report reads. “Even a dog, the family pet, was found tied up.” Three of the victims were shot in the head, authorities said; the other was shot in the back.


	Two men have been arrested in connection with the murders, according to a statement from Omar García Harfuch, the country’s secretary of public security. He said one of the suspects, partially identified by authorities as Diego Sebastián “N,” was a business partner of a victim and “allegedly used that relationship of trust to gain access to the residence.”


	“Today we honor and celebrate his life, his music, his light, and what he shared with those of us fortunate enough to know him and walk alongside him,” Camilo Séptimo wrote in social media posts. 

	Camilo Séptimo was formed in Mexico City in 2013 by Meléndez (pictured above, right) singer Manuel Mendoza and guitarist Erik Vázquez. The band released an EP in 2014 and its first album, “Óleos” (“oil paintings”) in 2017, which reached No. 10 on the Mexican albums charts. The group followed with three more albums, the most recent being 2023’s “Jardín de las almas” (“garden of souls”).  
	

	Variety will have more on the situation as it develops.

title: Joe Swanberg Sets Next Film: Shiloh Fernandez and Marc Senter Star in Chicago-Set Indie Rock Dramedy (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Indie auteur Joe Swanberg‘s is ready to rock.

	Swanberg is writing, editing and directing an as-yet-untitled 35mm dramedy in Chicago. Shiloh Fernan
body:
Indie auteur Joe Swanberg‘s is ready to rock.

	Swanberg is writing, editing and directing an as-yet-untitled 35mm dramedy in Chicago. Shiloh Fernandez and Marc Senter star as Oliver Cross and Lucas Hunter, founders of an indie rock band named Fast Star.

	Per the logline, “two longtime indie rock musicians’ band gets an unexpected second wind after a younger, newly popular rapper samples one of their old songs. Suddenly back in the spotlight and on tour, their increasingly different approaches to middle age push long-simmering personal and creative tensions to the breaking point.”
	

	Kali Skrap, Karley Sciortino and Chris Tuttle round out the cast. Kevin Veselka is the cinematographer on the feature.


	The film is a Last Encore and Ghost Gang production, in association with 3Links Productions. Senter, Ashleigh Snead, Nathan Crooker, Swanberg and Sean E. DeMott are producers on the project. Kathy Gitibin Parsa, Ariana Parsa, John Greenberg, Ray Blanchard and Anthony Killough are executive producers.

	Swanberg’s prolific career behind the camera includes “Drinking Buddies,” “Happy Christmas,” “Digging for Fire” and the Netflix anthology series “Easy.” His most recent film, “The Sun Never Sets,” stars Dakota Fanning and Jake Johnson. It debuted at SXSW before a theatrical release from Independent Film Company and Sapan Studio.

	Fernandez’s credits include “The Odyssey,” “The Basics of Philosophy” and “Evil Dead.” Senter has appeared in “Old Man,” “The Lost” and “Red, White & Blue.”

	Fernandez is repped by Jason Weinberg and Steven Nossokoff at Untitled Entertainment.
	

	See the first looks from the film above and below.

title: Telluride Festival Lineup: ‘The Debut,’ ‘Elsinore’ and ‘Tender Loving Care’ Set for Premieres, Tributes for John Malkovich, Sandra Hüller and Andrew Haigh
description: The Telluride Film Festival has unveiled the lineup for its 53rd edition, headlined by world-premiere titles starring Andrew Scott (“Elsinore”), Jul
body:
The Telluride Film Festival has unveiled the lineup for its 53rd edition, headlined by world-premiere titles starring Andrew Scott (“Elsinore”), Julianne Moore (“The Debut”) and Kate O’Flynn (“Tender Loving Care”), alongside new films from auteurs including Jordan Firstman (“Club Kid”), Joshua Oppenheimer (“The Revolution Against Death”) and Werner Herzog (“Bucking Fastard”).

	The festival will also pay tribute to three exemplary artists of cinema, along with their programmed feature films — actor John Malkovich (star of Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine”), actress Sandra Hüller (star of Paweł Pawlikowski’s “Fatherland” and Markus Schleinzer’s “Rose”) and writer-director Andrew Haigh, who helms the drama “A Long Winter,” making its world premiere.
	

	The Silver Medallion has become one of the awards season’s more dependable leading indicators, its honorees surfacing in the Oscar race with striking regularity. In each of the last four editions, at least one recipient has landed a major nomination, and several have won outright. Jane Campion took the medallion in 2021 and went on to win best director for “The Power of the Dog”; Sarah Polley followed in 2022 and won best adapted screenplay for “Women Talking,” the same year fellow honoree Cate Blanchett scored a best actress nomination for “Tár.” Yorgos Lanthimos (“Poor Things” in 2023) and Jacques Audiard (“Emilia Pérez” in 2024) each converted their tributes into director nominations.


	Also making its world premiere is Jennifer Peedom’s “Tenzing,” a retelling of the first successful ascent of Mount Everest starring Tom Hiddleston and newcomer Genden Phuntsok.
	

	Several titles arrive having already traveled the festival circuit this year, among them the Sundance hit “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” featuring veteran John Turturro — still awaiting his first Oscar nomination. French actress Léa Seydoux leads another circuit traveler from Cannes, Marie Kreutzer’s “Gentle Monster.” The film arrives alongside the Palme d’Or-winning drama “Fjord” from Cristian Mungiu, which stars Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve, and one of the best director winners, Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, with “La Bola Negra.”

	Some Venice titles are making the trek over from Italy in time for the Colorado mountains, such as the aforementioned Herzog and McDonagh with their films, as well as Danny Boyle’s newspaper drama “Ink” with Jack O’Connell and Guy Pearce, which opened the fest.



	

									Adam Newport-Berra
	



	For Julie Huntsinger, marking her 20th Telluride, the year carried echoes of a not-so-distant era — one in which modestly scaled films punched far above their weight. Read from a distance, the 2026 lineup gives off a distinct mood: AI dread, exile, authoritarianism, the ache of being alone together. Huntsinger sees all of it. She just doesn’t want anyone to forget the jokes.

	“My sense of humor is quite broad,” the festival director said, running through a program she has assembled. “Are we laughing harder in darkly tragic times? Yes. Or maybe we want to laugh more. I wish that comedies would be proliferating the way the genre films are. Why isn’t that happening?”

	Part of the answer, this year, is that a few of them are on the mountain. Alongside the dread sit the Zellner brothers’ “Alpha Gang” and Szumowska and Englert’s “The Idiot(s),” both among the program’s stranger surprises.

	Which raises the question every Telluride visitor eventually asks: Is the best picture winner up here? Huntsinger, playing along with Variety’s should-win/will-win Emmy prediction game, drew a careful line. “I definitely think the should-win is here,” she explains. “I don’t think the will-win is, because there is a Goliath out there that people are very smitten with.” She seemed to be referring to “The Odyssey,” though she didn’t name it directly.

	Huntsinger’s own list of don’t-miss titles runs long. She called Markus Schleinzer’s “Rose” and Paweł Pawlikowski’s “Fatherland” — both from Mubi — “two perfect movies,” professed love “with my whole heart” for Jordan Firstman’s “Club Kid” and threw in Boyle’s “Ink,” Mungiu’s “Fjord” and Aimee Lou Wood’s “so fun and so weird” performance in “The Idiot(s)” for good measure. Of the central performance in Guy Nattiv’s “The Liberation,” starring Carrie Coon, she urged audiences to “watch it multiple times to really understand how incredible this woman actually is.”
	

	This year’s documentary slate includes Ron Howard’s “Avedon,” Nanette Burstein’s “Carl Sagan: We Are Made of Star Stuff,” Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin’s “Everest: The Other Side,” Bryan Fogel’s “The Row,” Frank Marshall’s Pete Townshend portrait “Behind Blue Eyes” and Joshua Oppenheimer’s “The Revolution Against Death.”

	Actor-director Rebecca Hall serves as this year’s guest director, curating a personal sidebar that includes Kenneth Lonergan’s “Margaret,” Charlie Kaufman’s “Synecdoche, New York” and Joseph Losey’s “The Servant.”

	All eyes turn to Sunday night, where a lone “TBA” sits on the festival schedule — the only true wild card of the weekend, its title withheld until the lights go down. “You won’t know till you walk into the theater,” Huntsinger says. “The people in that room are going to be real, real lucky.” 

	The festival runs from Sept. 4-7. The full Telluride Film Festival lineup is below.

	Festivities

	“Wildwood: Inside the Frame” — Sheridan Opera House Gallery, Friday-Monday, 10 a.m.-5 p.m.

	For 20 years, Laika, whose animated feature films have been nominated for five Academy Awards, has pursued one idea above all else: that handmade films can move audiences in powerful and meaningful ways. “Wildwood,” Laika’s upcoming release, is the culmination of that pursuit. The exhibition showcases the cinematic language, emotional journey and creative processes that shaped the eagerly awaited film.

	Live Discussion With the Creators of “Wildwood” — Sheridan Opera House, Sunday, 1:15 p.m.

	The upcoming Laika film “Wildwood” grew from an innovative collaboration: director-producer and Laika president and CEO Travis Knight and celebrated cinematographer Caleb Deschanel, a six-time Academy Award nominee, approached the film’s stop-motion animation with the instincts of a live-action filmmaker.

	The result is a visual language unlike any previous Laika film, one that treats every puppet, every set and every frame as though they existed within a live-action movie. Knight, Deschanel and moderator Dave Karger of Turner Classic Movies will discuss the film and provide a Telluride-only sneak peek of key scenes before it is released in theaters on Oct. 23.

	Marfa Stance Studio: A Groundbreaking Collaboration — Telluride Science & Innovation Center, 300 S. Townsend, Friday-Sunday, 10 a.m.-5 p.m.; Monday, 10 a.m.-2 p.m.
	

	Marfa Stance, the British outerwear company whose modular garments evolve with you, brings its innovative process to the festival. Inspired by founder and designer Georgia Dant’s London studio, this installation showcases a new project: the Women Filmmakers Jacket.

	This evolving garment was shaped by conversations with directors, producers, cinematographers, and creatives across the international film industry. Designed for the realities of women on set, the jacket serves as a symbol of collaboration, visibility and presence, celebrating the creativity, resilience and leadership of women in film.

	Women Directors Roundtable — Marfa Stance Studio, Sunday, 3 p.m.

	Festival Director Julie Huntsinger will host a panel of distinguished filmmakers. In this first-of-its-kind discussion at Telluride, these acclaimed women leaders in film will share their creative visions and describe their successes and challenges.

	Step Inside the F-Stop — Mountain Village, Friday-Monday, 9 a.m.-5 p.m.

	Don’t miss the immersive traveling Airstream experience celebrating the bold, auteur-driven cinema of Focus Features. Featuring “Elsinore” and inspired by the legacy of Telluride favorites such as “Brokeback Mountain,” “Hamnet,” “Conclave” and “The Holdovers,” the space offers engaging visuals, exclusive merchandise and a creative respite between screenings.

	Filmmaking and Technology With Empathy: AI for Societal Benefit — Telluride Science & Innovation Center, 300 S. Townsend, Sunday, 9 a.m.

	Join Primordial Soup and the creative team behind “Love, Rendered” for an insider’s look at how the team documented the realities of cognitive decline and memory loss with a multigenerational family using cutting-edge AI technology to unlock previously “lost” moments.

	Through an ongoing strategic partnership with Google DeepMind, Primordial Soup (“Goodnight Lamby,” “Ancestra”) is an AI-driven creative studio founded in 2025 that merges bold narrative, emotional depth and experimental workflows to develop original stories and the tools to tell them.
	

	“The Humanity Dilemma” — Sheridan Opera House, Saturday, 11 a.m.

	Made possible by a donation from Melony and Adam Lewis, with additional support from Marni Grossman.

	From the team behind “The Social Dilemma,” “The AI Dilemma” and “The AI Doc,” Tristan Harris, Joy Mauthe and Aza Raskin present a multimedia experience that explores the defining invention of our time.

	Blending original music, live projections and narration with sharp insight, it explores the “species-level event” of AI’s birth, the race accelerating beneath it and what’s required of us now. Is an AI-dominated future inevitable? This talk offers grounded, non-naive hope for a different path.

title: ‘Bucking Fastard’ Review: Herner Werzog’s Uddled-Mup Fairytale Stars the Mara Sisters as You’ve Never Seen Her Before
description: Occasionally sublime, often ridiculous and always extravagantly weird, Werner Herzog‘s “Bucking Fastard,” unlike its gorgeously interlinked protagon
body:
Occasionally sublime, often ridiculous and always extravagantly weird, Werner Herzog‘s “Bucking Fastard,” unlike its gorgeously interlinked protagonists, is a film of multiple personalities that only rarely speak in unison. Kate and Rooney Mara, appearing together — oh so together — for the first time, are endlessly fascinating playing two sisters who speak and react simultaneously and identically, less a pair of people than a palimpsest of a single person. This unprecedented duality is not simply a casting and acting coup, it is rich with potential meaning and mood: there is something inexpressibly sad and beautiful about the ideas it prompts, about the loneliness of the human condition, about the polite savagery of society towards its outliers, about the nature of kinship and whether it’s possible — and maybe even enviable — for two people to share one soul, the way they might share a teapot. 
	

	But this is Werner Herzog, and by God and the fundamentally chaotic nature of the Universe, Herzog gonna Herzog. And so, despite the already richly strange premise, there must also be dream sequences in which fluttering birds twitter madly in their cages, sidebars about sneering hunters culling probably-not-rabid foxes and baroque digressions about the genome of the cave salamander. With Ernst Reijseger’s wonderfully varied score keeping pace, through folk fiddle and classical cello and stretches of wondering, wandering piano, there just have to be touches of fairytale and a dose of Looney Tunes. For some reason we need loads of quasi-mythological musings on the nature of devotion and whole lot of mummery about the Orkney Islands, all stuffed into a narrative that becomes increasingly estranged from anything resembling a reality to which we might usefully return, arms laden, with all these new splendors to relate.
	

	Herzog’s script is inspired, partially, by his meeting Freda and Greta Chaplin, twin sisters whose unique and inexplicable manner of speaking, in addition to their anti-social behavior, gave them some minor U.K. notoriety in the 1980s. Transposed to Ireland — or rather, to a skewed and fantastical idea of Ireland — they become Jeanie (Kate Mara) and Joanie (Rooney Mara), the Holbrooke sisters, who as the film begins are up in court after a restraining order has been filed against them. Making much of the “precedent” he is setting in Irish law, the judge (Simon Delaney) allows both sisters to take the stand together and to give evidence as one — our first taste of the Maras’ remarkable mirroring-and-matching abilities.

	The case has been brought by their neighbor, Mr Mulroney, with whom the two women, as one, believe themselves completely, forever-and-ever in love. (The Holbrookes are simultaneously childlike and horny as hell.) Limo driver Mulroney has indeed been enjoying their sexual favors, with the cat-who-got-the-cream smugness of, well, a man who has a regular threesome going with two comely if somewhat oddball sisters. He’s played by Orlando Bloom, who really does look the part of the heartbreaker-gone-a-bit-to-seed. He even quite sounds the part too, except when he stumbles up against a long “i” and his Irish accent swerves into Oirish. Anyway, Mulroney recently ended things with the girls in order to get married, which cued several fanciful attempts at revenge, which continue well after the trial has ended. During one such act of whimsical vandalism, as they set a letterbox on fire under the impression that it will prevent Mulroney from sending love letters to his wife, they are witnessed by another neighbor, kindly Mr Westmoreland (John Kavanagh).

	Rather than being even mildly fazed, Westmoreland is one in a long line of (mostly) men whose protective instincts are stirred by these strange apparations, in their matching ankle-length chambray dresses, their matchingly shapeless cardigans and matching embroidered handbags, slung over opposite arms — the better to walk in lockstep, elbow touching elbow. (Props to costume designer Maeve Paterson for giving them a frumpy Tradwife aesthetic that is, after a while, a real look). He offers them a refuge in the city — if it’s Dublin it is, again, the unrecognisably quaint Dublin of Herzog’s imagination rather than a place its inhabitants might deem authentic — in a turret-like top room, where they can be visited by the lonely widower and by their social worker, Timothy (a lovely, gentle and too-brief turn from Domhnall Gleeson).
	

	Other men on the street and at work in the surroundings alternately lust after and spy on the sisters. One passerby even cajoles them into taking a selfie for his socials, a jolting moment when we realise that all of this is supposedly taking place in the present day, despite letterboxes and old-lady headscarves still being a thing and nobody appearing to have a TV. No matter, soon their Aunt Louise writes to invite them back to the countryside, where to all intents and purposes, it is the past: There, they can farm and ramble and spend their evenings crotcheting by the fireside. And behind that Sligo farmstead looms spectacular, cave-speckled Keshcorran Hill, where the sisters, and DP Peter Zeitlinger’s wistfully magic-tinged photography, will find their final purpose.

	It feels almost heretical to wish that a Werner Herzog film were just a little less outlandish. But while “Bucking Fastard” gives us, in the Mara sisters’ uncannily synced-up performances, a novelty worth the price of admission alone, it is mired in so much mythology and mystery that by the end, the fact of the sisters being two who respond and react as one becomes all but immaterial. If anything, perhaps it’s born of fondness: Herzog has amassed a rogues’ gallery of freaks and madmen and outcasts in his back catalogue, but seldom has he dealt with any of them this kindly, this sweetly and with this little hard-edged insight into why they behave the way that they do.

	It is a shame, because the loopy, fantasy-tinged episodes in which they end up embroiled are never as thrilling or as moving as the simpler moments, as when four hands gracefully pour tea from a single pot, or when two hands compose a letter in tandem but in different handwriting, or when the pair ignore their reflections and instead use the other as a mirror by which to knot their matching headscarves just so. Instead of probing, or even further observing, this intricate psychology, Herzog becomes preoccupied with the sisters’ dream of escape to a “better world than this one,” to “Arcadia or Atlantis or Orkney.” That they actually end up in a Slovenian rock formation full of stalactites and chandeliers is quite literally neither here nor there, for a story whose coherence has long since disappeared into the caves and forgotten dreams — now remembered — of Werner Herzog’s magpie mind.

schema.headline: ‘Bucking Fastard’ Review: Herner Werzog’s Uddled-Mup Fairytale Stars the Mara Sisters as You’ve Never Seen Her Before

title: Josh Peck to Host Food Network’s Tasting-Required Take on ‘Is It Cake?’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Food Network has found its answer to Netflix’s “Is It Cake?”

	Premiering with back-to-back episodes Oct. 5 at 10 p.m. ET on Food Network and stream
body:
Food Network has found its answer to Netflix’s “Is It Cake?”

	Premiering with back-to-back episodes Oct. 5 at 10 p.m. ET on Food Network and streaming next day on HBO Max, “Sweet Deceit” is a competition series hosted by actor Josh Peck, who leads teams of three competitors through four rounds as they try to identify masterfully disguised sweets created by world-class cake artists. 


	But unlike Netflix’s guessing game, “Sweet Deceit” takes place in real-world locations and requires its contestants to take a bite to decipher the deceptive, hyperrealistic sweets hiding in plain sight.
	

	Per Food Network’s description, “Escalating in difficulty round by round, the teams work together to determine what is cake and prove it with their teeth by biting into their best guess, all in pursuit of a total prize up to $12,000.”


	The first season will be broken up into two themed batches of episodes.

	Beginning on Oct. 5 at 10 p.m. ET, “Sweet Deceit: Trick or Treat” features eight back-to-back Halloween-themed episodes set in locations including real-life haunted houses, a sinister movie set morgue, a kindergarten classroom Halloween party, the world-famous Magic Castle and more. 

	“Sweet Deceit: Holiday” will premiere Nov. 16 at 9 p.m. ET. The installment will be comprised of eight back-to-back episodes featuring locations including a cozy cabin, a festive ice rink, Santa’s workshop and more. 

	Peck will be joined by a rotating group of guest stars made up of several cake artists specializing in edible illusions, including Jose Barajas, Jonny “Jonny Cakes” Manganello, Andrew Fuller, Ashley Holt, April Julian and Liz Marek.
	

	“’Sweet Deceit’ has all my favorite things: food, fun, and deception,” Peck said. “The craftsmanship our cake artists put into their creations was unlike anything I’ve ever seen — the edible creations are unbelievable, watching teams literally put their money where their mouths are made every reveal a blast. It’s a must watch for the whole family.”

	Food Network president Betsy Ayala added: “’Sweet Deceit’ is a funny and highly visual new game show that puts a hilarious twist on the art of illusion and is the perfect addition to Food Network’s baking lineup. Josh Peck is the perfect host to bring humor to every reveal and fans will be amazed and shocked by what turns out to be edible as they guess alongside the teams from home.”

	“Sweet Deceit” is produced by Lando Entertainment for Food Network.

schema.headline: Josh Peck to Host Food Network’s Tasting-Required Take on ‘Is It Cake?’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Neon Sets 1,500-Theater U.S. Release for Na Hong-Jin’s ‘Hope,’ Widest for Korean Film Since ‘Parasite’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Neon will release Na Hong-Jin‘s “Hope” in some 1,500 U.S. theaters starting Sept. 9, marking the widest domestic theatrical footprint for a Korean-l
body:
Neon will release Na Hong-Jin‘s “Hope” in some 1,500 U.S. theaters starting Sept. 9, marking the widest domestic theatrical footprint for a Korean-language film since the studio’s 2019 Best Picture winner “Parasite.”

	The rollout builds on Neon’s recent pattern of securing expansive U.S. launches for Korean and other international-language titles, including “No Other Choice” and “Oldboy,” bringing filmmakers the studio considers among world cinema’s strongest auteurs to wider domestic audiences.
	

	Ahead of the wide bow, “Hope” will screen in early access showings on Sept. 7 across several premium large-format setups – among them Dolby, 4DX, ScreenX, Barco HDR and D-BOX venues, plus Dolby Atmos sound presentations. Several of those screenings have already sold out, and presales are strong in New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Austin and San Francisco, among other markets. Tickets for the early access event are on sale now.


	“Hope” is led by an international ensemble featuring “Squid Game” star and Emmy nominee Hoyeon, alongside Hwang Jung-min, Zo In-sung, Taylor Russell, Cameron Britton, Vikander and Fassbender. The film has already become one of South Korea’s highest-grossing releases of the year and premiered at the Cannes Film Festival, where it emerged as one of the festival’s most talked-about genre entries.

	The Variety review described it as “featuring some of the most breathtakingly elegant action moviemaking of this or any year.” “Hope” marks Na Hong-Jin’s return to feature filmmaking after a 10-year hiatus; the director is previously known for “The Wailing” and “The Chaser.”
	

	The story unfolds in Hope Harbor, an isolated coastal town in South Korea, after a mysterious creature begins terrorizing residents. Police and local hunters set out to track the animal down, only to find themselves the ones being hunted, touching off a chain of events with devastating consequences.

	“Hope” is produced by Forged Films, with Plus M Entertainment and Westworld coming aboard as co-producers. Plus M Entertainment presents and distributes the film, with Neon handling its North American theatrical release beginning Sept. 9.

	Neon has earned 57 Academy Award nominations in nine years, including Best Picture wins for “Anora” and “Parasite,” which earned $53.8 million in North America. The studio received 18 Oscar nominations this year, the second-most of any motion picture studio, with “Sentimental Value” and “The Secret Agent” both nominated for Best Picture and “Sentimental Value” winning Best International Film. Neon has also taken home the Palme d’Or from Cannes for seven consecutive years, most recently for “Fjord.”

schema.headline: Neon Sets 1,500-Theater U.S. Release for Na Hong-Jin’s ‘Hope,’ Widest for Korean Film Since ‘Parasite’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Asian Male Pageantry Gets Unscripted Competition Series Based on Microdrama-Turned-Feature Franchise ‘Rags 2 Richmond’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Viral Nation and Media Trifecta have teamed up to develop an unscripted competition series built around Octagon Metatainment‘s “Rags 2 Richmond” fra
body:
Viral Nation and Media Trifecta have teamed up to develop an unscripted competition series built around Octagon Metatainment‘s “Rags 2 Richmond” franchise. 

	Buyers will get their first look at the series at the Access Canada Summit, held as part of the Toronto Film Festival’s inaugural market.

	The series translates the world of Asian male pageantry into a rags-to-riches competition format. Contestants face challenges built around performance, style, talent and showmanship as they transform their look and image, before a live pageant finale crowns a winner.
	

	Media Trifecta’s Kevin Healey, chief creative officer, and Sharone Ostrovsky, chief executive, are steering the project alongside Viral Nation programming chief Paul Telner and an Octagon Metatainment team led by Justina Shih, Simon Yin, Jonathan Wong and Dylan St Aubin.


	“From the beginning, we believed ‘Rags 2 Richmond’ had the potential to become much more than a vertical series,” said Telner. “Jonathan and the team created a story that resonated because it was authentic, culturally specific, and deeply personal – anchored by an incredible soundtrack. At Viral Nation, we’re focused on helping creators transform their ideas into scalable entertainment properties, and ‘Rags 2 Richmond’ is a powerful example of how creator-led IP can evolve across formats into enduring franchises.”

	The franchise grew out of Wong, Shih and Yin’s own experiences competing in and observing Asian beauty pageants and talent contests held across North America and Asia. Canadians make up an estimated 40% of the winners in that circuit, many of them from Richmond, British Columbia, which inspired the franchise’s name.
	

	As a vertical series, the property ranked among the top-performing independent titles in the microdrama category, pulling in over nine million views on Instagram within its debut month. Distribution followed through Viddsee, along with brand tie-ins involving Air Canada and K-Swiss.

	“‘Rags 2 Richmond’ represents the next generation of entertainment franchises – stories that begin with creators, build passionate audiences, and expand organically across formats,” said Healey. “We’re excited to partner with Viral Nation, Jonathan Wong, and Justina Shih to bring this next chapter of the ‘Rags 2 Richmond’ universe to life through competition-format storytelling.”

	Ostrovsky said she was drawn to the project by its stories and its look inside a world most North American audiences know little about, despite its popularity across Asia. “Working with the star-level producing teams behind ‘Rags 2 Richmond’ and Viral Nation has felt like everything creating should be about: passion, storytelling, risk-taking,” she said. “We’re thrilled to introduce this next chapter to buyers at the Access Canada Summit.”

	The franchise’s move into feature film came earlier this year, with Wong topping the cast. That cast is led by Wong, joined by Eric Tsang (“Infernal Affairs”), Nancy Sit (“God of Cookery”), Shannon Kook (“The Conjuring”) and Jennifer Tong (“Fakes”). That production wrapped in late 2025, and the film is set to screen at the Toronto market while distribution talks continue.

	“This project started as a proof of concept online, because entertainment decision-makers had no frame of reference for what it could become,” Wong said. “But when a passionate global community of champions and supporters started to form around the music and storytelling, we knew we were onto something.”

	“Speaking as a local, what’s been accomplished here in the past two years is unique, both in vision and speed,” said St Aubin, who worked on the vertical series as an editor before producing the feature film. “Jon, Justina, and Simon arrived with the goal of elevating our city and its talent on their own merits, and the momentum they’ve achieved – from a vertical series, to a feature film, and now a competition series – has given us a global platform in record time. There’s a proven infrastructure in Vancouver that deserves to be tapped, and this team’s fresh perspective has set that in motion in meaningful fashion.”
	

	K-Swiss’s role in the franchise has grown as well, shifting from a product placement in the film to commissioning Wong for an anthem marking the brand’s 60th anniversary.

schema.headline: Asian Male Pageantry Gets Unscripted Competition Series Based on Microdrama-Turned-Feature Franchise ‘Rags 2 Richmond’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Technoblade Never Dies’ Documentary Film About Late Minecraft Content Creator in the Works With Funding From Riot Games and Hypixel Studios
description: The life and legacy of Technoblade, the beloved and influential Minecraft creator who died in 2022, will be chronicled in a feature-length documenta
body:
The life and legacy of Technoblade, the beloved and influential Minecraft creator who died in 2022, will be chronicled in a feature-length documentary film.

	Titled “Technoblade Never Dies” — a catchphrase of the late California-based creator — the project is being made with the full support and cooperation of Technoblade’s family. The film is being produced by Candle Media’s Candle True Stories with financing from Riot Games and Hypixel Studios, both of which will donate their profits from the film to charity. Hypixel Studios is an independent game studio founded by the team behind Hypixel, the world’s biggest Minecraft server.
	

	The film is intended to be “an independent feature documentary to bring Technoblade’s story and community to audiences around the world,” according to Candle True Stories.


	“Technoblade Never Dies” is just entering production and there is no release date yet. The film’s producers say the plan is to premiere it at a major festival, followed by a theatrical release and then broader distribution (with a distribution deal yet to be secured).

	Directed by documentary maker Steven Lake, “Technoblade Never Dies” promises to tell for the first time the story of the young man behind the legendary online alter ego. Per Candle True Stories’ description: “Through intimate access to his family and friends, hundreds of hours of Technoblade’s own content, and stories from the massive global community he inspired, the film will explore how a shy and anonymous California teenager transformed himself into a Minecraft warrior whose humor, skill and singular personality captured the hearts of millions.”
	

	Technoblade’s community remains active today: His YouTube channel currently has nearly 23 million subscribers, and his influence persists across gaming culture — including a tribute to his iconic crowned-pig avatar in 2025’s “A Minecraft Movie.”

	Technoblade began creating Minecraft videos as a teenager with the dream of reaching 10 million subscribers to his YouTube channel, a goal he achieved in late 2021, just months before his death.

	In 2021, Technoblade revealed his cancer diagnosis and continued communicating with fans throughout treatment with the humor and resilience that defined him. Following his death in June 2022 at the age of 23, his father shared his final message, “so long nerds,” revealing his son’s name for the first time: Alex. (The family has kept their identity private.)

	In addition to Technoblade’s own life and experiences, the film will also explore the community he left behind and the bond it has formed with his family, particularly his father, Marshall, who became known to fans as “Mr. Technodad.”

	Following Technoblade’s death, more than 400,000 messages from fans were collected in a virtual Minecraft memorial and transformed into 22 books of condolences for his family. The film will explore the “extraordinary relationship between creator and community, weaving together stories from fans around the world whose lives were shaped by Technoblade and showing how an online fandom became a real-world source of friendship, connection and collective grief,” per Candle True Stories.

	“’Technoblade Never Dies’ is an endearing and authentic exploration of the positive power of the internet and video games,” Lake said in a statement. “The Technoblade story is a triumphant exploration of the echo that the ones we love leave behind.”

	“Technoblade Never Dies” is produced by Max Heckman for Candle True Stories, Robert Ford and Steven Lake. James Goldston serves as executive producer for Candle True Stories.

	Candle True Stories is part of Candle Media, the media holding company co-founded by former Disney execs Kevin Mayer and Tom Staggs. Candle True Stories produces premium, scripted and nonscripted content for a variety of formats and platforms, including 2026 titles for Netflix, “Should I Marry a Murderer?” and “Michael Jackson: The Verdict.” Prior projects include two series for Paramount+, “Wild Boys: Strangers In Town” and “The Carters,” as well as a U.K. version of ABC News’ “20/20” and Netflix’s “Untold: The Liver King.”

schema.headline: ‘Technoblade Never Dies’ Documentary Film About Late Minecraft Content Creator in the Works With Funding From Riot Games and Hypixel Studios

title: Dave Bautista Shows Off Body Transformation to Play Kratos in ‘God of War’ Series: ‘Two More Months to Get to Where I Need to Be’
description:
Sep 3, 2026 7:08am PT	
	

	
		Dave Bautista Shows Off Body Transformation to Play Kratos in ‘God of War’ Series: ‘Two More Months to G
body:
Sep 3, 2026 7:08am PT	
	

	
		Dave Bautista Shows Off Body Transformation to Play Kratos in ‘God of War’ Series: ‘Two More Months to Get to Where I Need to Be’
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Dave Bautista Instagram / PlayStation
	

		
	
				
	Dave Bautista is back in the gym and showing off his muscle gains to play the super-strong Greek hero Kratos in the upcoming adaptation of the “God of War” video game. The actor shared a video of himself flexing in the gym and revealed that he’s three weeks into his weight training regime, with two more months to go.

	“Third week in to weight training again. Two more months to get to where I need to be. Like ridin’ a bike!” he wrote as he gave a very Kratos-inspired roar into the camera while music played.
	


	Bautista officially signed on to play Kratos on Aug. 20, taking the reigns from Ryan Hurst after the original actor suffered an on-set injury and Prime Video recast the role. Hurst tore his bicep on set and needed surgery that would have delayed restarting production into 2027. Filming originally began in Vancouver back in February, and all the scenes with Hurst will have to be reshot with Bautista. Prime Video gave “God of War” a two-season order, with the two seasons set to shoot back-to-back.


	The series will follow the story of the two most recent “God of War” games, in which Kratos must raise his ten-year old son Atreus (played by young actor Callum Vinson) while battling gods of the Norse pantheon. Per the logline, “Father and son Kratos and Atreus embark on a journey to spread the ashes of their wife and mother, Faye. Through their adventures, Kratos tries to teach his son to be a better god, while Atreus tries to teach his father how to be a better human.” 

	Bautista, a WWE veteran and mixed martial artist, is no stranger to playing large, muscular characters. He starred as Drax the Destroyer in several “Guardians of the Galaxy” and “Avengers” movies, and he’ll next appear in “Road House 2” and the “Highlander” reboot.


	
		More from Variety

title: 'Survivor Greece' Injured Contestant Stavros Floros Sues For $100 Million Over Losing Leg While Filming
description:
'Survivor Greece'
                          Contestant Stavros Floros Sues Producers
body:
'Survivor Greece'
                          Contestant Stavros Floros Sues Producers
                          For $100 Million After Losing Leg On Show
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 3, 2026
                            7:01 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 3, 2026
                                7:51 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
            "Survivor Greece" star Stavros Floros is suing producers of the reality show over an accident during the production that resulted in his left leg being severed above the knee ... and he's seeking 9 figures in damages ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to court docs, obtained by TMZ, Stavros, who appeared on the Greek version of the popular series, was filming when a tour boat propeller struck him while he was spearfishing for food on May 11, 2026.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            He claims the producers built the show’s entire format around requiring the contestants to spearfish in open water -- waters he says were heavily trafficked by tourist boats near the area they filmed.
      

            He claims there were no safety boats, protected zones, or adequate warning markers ... despite prior close calls and even a death in the same waters.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Stavros said his leg was lost in the ocean and that only a “tourniquet applied by a stranger aboard the offending tourist boat kept him alive.”
      
    
            The reality star was transported to a Miami hospital, where he underwent multiple surgeries over a 61-day hospitalization.
      
    
            Stavros is seeking over $100 million in damages for the incident on set.

body:

                          New Baby, New $2.2M Home!!!

            Blueface has a new baby ... and now, a new home for his growing family ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Sources familiar with the sale ... the rapper recently moved into a sprawling $2.25 million property in Moorpark, California ... just in time for the arrival of his newborn son.
